blocks.text:
**Jaundice, pale stools or dark urine:** not isolated — fractionated bilirubin and hepatology today.
**Fever with bone pain, or refuses to bear weight:** emergency department now — infection or leukemia.
**Night bone pain, limp, bone swelling or a mass, weight loss:** today — X-ray, CBC with smear; oncology if a lesion or abnormal smear. A normal X-ray does not exclude leukemia.
**Seizure, tetany or stridor in a child with possible rickets:** emergency department now — calcium.
**Sick, jaundiced child with a LOW ALP and Coombs-negative hemolysis:** think acute Wilson disease — INR now, call hepatology / transplant center now.

Cholestatic liver disease — raised GGT means liver
Leukemia — bone pain or limp with a normal X-ray: CBC with smear

Hypophosphatasia — ALP LOW for age, early tooth loss
Zinc deficiency — lowers ALP and can hide cholestasis
Acute Wilson disease — low ALP, hemolysis, jaundice

blocks.text:
ALP comes from liver (canalicular membrane), bone, intestine, placenta and kidney. In children, bone dominates: rapid bone growth keeps ALP well above adult levels (ACG 2017; BSG 2018), highest in the pubertal spurt (lesson 01-01). Read against an adult range, almost every growing child looks high.

GGT is in liver and bile ducts but not in bone. ACG and BSG both use it to decide whether a raised ALP comes from the liver; ALP isoenzymes do the same when GGT is unhelpful. BSG suggests — without data — that an isolated ALP rise without symptoms is most often vitamin D deficiency or normal growth.

Transient hyperphosphatasemia (THI) is probably the commonest cause of a very high ALP in a well infant or toddler. In 813 published cases, ALP was ≥ 5 × ULN in about 70%; it was back to normal within 4 months in 80% and took longer in about 20%. It often follows an infection and affects 1.1–3.5% of children aged 2–24 months (Gualco 2013). Recognizing it avoids imaging and biopsies.

A low ALP is also abnormal. Hypophosphatasia (ALPL variants) is diagnosed late: in a global registry, children's first sign came at a median 7.2 months and diagnosis at 20.4 months (Högler 2019). ALP is a zinc enzyme, so zinc deficiency lowers it (Khan 2024; lesson 01-01). In acute Wilson disease, a low ALP beside hemolysis and jaundice is a classic clue (Korman 2008).

items.text: An adult ALP range flags almost every growing child. Use the lab's range for age and sex.
GGT first: raised GGT = liver; normal GGT = bone or other (ACG 2017; BSG 2018).
Well toddler, ALP in the thousands, everything else normal: THI. Repeat in 3–4 months, nothing else (Gualco 2013).
GGT is high in young infants and lowest at 1–6 years — below adult values. A GGT "normal" for an adult can be raised in a toddler (lesson 01-01).
Low ALP for age is never "normal". Think hypophosphatasia, zinc deficiency and, in a sick jaundiced child, Wilson disease (Khan 2024).
Hypophosphatasia: early non-traumatic loss of baby teeth, root intact, is a major clue. Raised PLP (vitamin B6) supports it (Khan 2024).
In a cholestatic child, a "normal" ALP may be zinc deficiency. Check zinc before you trust it.
ALP is not a reliable marker of bile duct injury in children — a normal-for-age ALP does not exclude it. Use GGT (ESPGHAN 2025).
